gale-crater.about: Impact crater about 154 km wide. Curiosity landed here in August 2012. At its center stands Mount Sharp (Aeolis Mons), a layered mound about 5 km high.
gale-crater.geology: Layered sedimentary rocks (mudstone and sandstone) deposited by water and wind over a long period.
gale-crater.importance: Curiosity found that Gale once had conditions that could support microbial life, including liquid water and key chemical elements. The layers record how Mars changed over time.

olympus-mons.about: The largest known volcano in the solar system, in the Tharsis region. It is about 600 km wide and roughly 22 km high, about two and a half times the height of Mount Everest.
olympus-mons.geology: Shield volcano built from many basaltic lava flows. It has a summit caldera and steep cliffs (scarps) around its base.
olympus-mons.importance: Shows how a planet without moving tectonic plates can build huge volcanoes. It is also a key reference for Mars volcanic history and a challenge for landing because of its altitude.

arsia-mons.about: Southernmost of the three large Tharsis Montes volcanoes. It is about 270 km wide and around 20 km high, with a summit caldera over 100 km wide.
arsia-mons.geology: Basaltic shield volcano. Its flanks include lava tubes and cave-like openings (skylights).
arsia-mons.importance: Lava tubes could shelter future explorers from radiation and temperature swings, and may protect ancient traces of life.

elysium-mons.about: Large volcano in the Elysium region, in the northern hemisphere, standing roughly 14 km above the Martian reference level.
elysium-mons.geology: Volcanic cone built by lava flows, with channels and flow features around it.
elysium-mons.importance: Marks a second major volcanic region besides Tharsis and is close to the InSight landing area.

valles-marineris.about: Largest canyon system known in the solar system, about 4,000 km long, up to several hundred km wide and up to about 7 km deep, near the Martian equator.
valles-marineris.geology: Formed mainly by stretching and cracking of the crust linked to the growth of the Tharsis volcanic region, then shaped by landslides and erosion. Layered walls expose old rock.
valles-marineris.importance: Its walls reveal a deep record of Mars geology. Minerals formed with water make it an interesting target, and its length makes it a landmark for route planning.

hellas-planitia.about: One of the largest impact basins on Mars, about 2,300 km across and roughly 7 km deep, in the southern hemisphere.
hellas-planitia.geology: Huge impact basin filled with sediments and dust. It is among the lowest places on the planet.
hellas-planitia.importance: Atmospheric pressure is highest at the lowest altitudes, so Hellas is studied for temperature, weather, and possible shelter from radiation.

viking-2.about: NASA's Viking 2 lander touched down on 3 September 1976 in Utopia Planitia, in the northern plains, and operated until 1980.
viking-2.geology: Flat plain covered with rocks and fine soil. Viking 2 photographed frost on the ground in winter.
viking-2.importance: Part of the first mission to successfully operate on the surface of Mars for a long time. It sent the first long-term weather and surface images, and ran experiments to look for life.

insight.about: NASA's InSight lander arrived on 26 November 2018 in Elysium Planitia, a flat plain near the equator, and operated until December 2022.
insight.geology: Smooth, sandy plain chosen for safe landing and stable conditions for instruments.
insight.importance: Its seismometer recorded hundreds of marsquakes, which allowed scientists to measure the thickness of the crust and the size of the Martian core.
